## Martingale Representation Theorem

The **martingale representation theorem** states that every square-integrable
[[martingale-theory|martingale]] in the filtration generated by a Brownian
motion is an [[ito-integral|Itô integral]] with respect to that Brownian
motion. Equivalently, the only source of randomness in such a filtration is
the Brownian motion itself, and all information is carried by its increments.

In [[quantitative-finance]] this is the reason that a market driven by
Brownian motion is **complete**: every contingent claim can be written as a
stochastic integral, which is the gain of a self-financing hedging strategy.

## Setup

Let $W=(W^1,\dots,W^n)$ be an $n$-dimensional
[[brownian-motion|Brownian motion]] on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ and
let $\mathbb{F}=(\mathcal{F}_t)$ be its natural filtration, augmented by the
$\mathbb{P}$-null sets (see [[filtrations-and-adapted-processes]]). Fix $T>0$
and write $\mathcal{L}^2$ for the space of progressively measurable processes
$g=(g^1,\dots,g^n)$ with

$$
\mathbb{E}\int_0^T |g_s|^2\,ds < \infty.
$$

For $g\in\mathcal{L}^2$ the Itô integral
$\int_0^t g_s\,dW_s=\sum_{i=1}^n\int_0^t g^i_s\,dW^i_s$ is a square-integrable
martingale and satisfies the **Itô isometry**

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\int_0^T g_s\,dW_s\right)^2\right]
= \mathbb{E}\int_0^T |g_s|^2\,ds.
$$

## The Theorem

:::{.theorem data-title="Itô Representation Theorem"}

For every $F\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_T,\mathbb{P})$ there is a unique
$g\in\mathcal{L}^2$ such that

$$
F = \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T g_s\,dW_s \quad \text{a.s.}
$$

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Martingale Representation Theorem"}

Let $M=(M_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ be an $\mathbb{F}$-martingale with
$\mathbb{E}[M_T^2]<\infty$. Then there is a unique $g\in\mathcal{L}^2$ such
that

$$
M_t = M_0 + \int_0^t g_s\,dW_s
\quad \text{for all } t\in[0,T], \text{ a.s.}
$$

In particular $M_0=\mathbb{E}[M_T]$ is constant and $M$ has a continuous
version.

:::

If $M$ is square integrable on $[0,t]$ for every $t\ge 0$, the processes $g$
obtained on different intervals agree by uniqueness, which gives a single $g$
on $[0,\infty)$.

## Proof

The martingale representation theorem follows from the Itô representation
theorem, which we prove first. The strategy is to show that the claim holds for
a family of random variables whose span is dense in $L^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$, and
then pass to the limit using the Itô isometry.

### Step 1: Exponentials are Total

For a bounded deterministic function $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ define

$$
Y^h_t = \exp\left( \int_0^t h_s\cdot dW_s
- \frac12\int_0^t |h_s|^2\,ds \right).
$$

:::{.theorem data-title="Lemma 1"}

The linear span of $\{Y^h_T : h \text{ a bounded deterministic step function}\}$
is dense in $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_T,\mathbb{P})$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Since the span is a linear subspace, it is dense if its orthogonal complement
is $\{0\}$. Let $g\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$ be orthogonal to every $Y^h_T$, that
is $\mathbb{E}[g\,Y^h_T]=0$. Since $Y^h_T$ is $\exp\left(\int_0^T h\cdot
dW\right)$ times a positive constant, this says

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[g\,\exp\left(\int_0^T h_s\cdot dW_s\right)\right] = 0.
$$

Fix times $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_m\le T$ and let $Z$ be the vector of increments
$W_{t_j}-W_{t_{j-1}}$, $j=1,\dots,m$, which lies in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with
$N=nm$. Taking $h=\sum_j\lambda_j\mathbf{1}_{(t_{j-1},t_j]}$ with
$\lambda_j\in\mathbb{R}^n$ gives

$$
\phi(\lambda) := \mathbb{E}\left[g\,e^{\lambda\cdot Z}\right] = 0
\quad \text{for all } \lambda\in\mathbb{R}^N.
$$

Because $Z$ is Gaussian it has exponential moments of all orders, so by
Cauchy-Schwarz the expectation is finite for complex $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^N$
and $\phi$ is an analytic function on $\mathbb{C}^N$. It vanishes on
$\mathbb{R}^N$, hence on all of $\mathbb{C}^N$. In particular
$\mathbb{E}[g\,e^{iy\cdot Z}]=0$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}^N$. This says that the
finite signed measure $\nu(A)=\mathbb{E}[g\,\mathbf{1}_{\{Z\in A\}}]$ on
$\mathbb{R}^N$ has zero Fourier transform, so $\nu=0$. Therefore
$\mathbb{E}[g\,\mathbf{1}_A]=0$ for every $A\in\sigma(Z)$.

The $\sigma$-algebras $\sigma(Z)$, over all choices of times, form a
$\pi$-system that generates $\mathcal{F}_T$ (up to null sets). By the
$\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem, $\mathbb{E}[g\,\mathbf{1}_A]=0$ for all
$A\in\mathcal{F}_T$, and hence $g=0$ almost surely.
:::

### Step 2: Representation of Exponentials

Let $h$ be a bounded deterministic step function. By [[ito-formula]] applied to
$\exp$ of the process $\int_0^t h\cdot dW-\frac12\int_0^t|h|^2ds$,

$$
dY^h_t = Y^h_t\,h_t\cdot dW_t,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
Y^h_T = 1 + \int_0^T Y^h_s\,h_s\cdot dW_s.
$$

Here $Y^h_s h_s\in\mathcal{L}^2$, since $h$ is bounded and
$\mathbb{E}[(Y^h_s)^2]=\exp\left(\int_0^s|h|^2\right)$ is bounded on $[0,T]$.
Since $\mathbb{E}[Y^h_T]=1$, this is the representation in the theorem for
$F=Y^h_T$. By linearity, the representation also holds for every finite linear
combination of the $Y^h_T$.

### Step 3: Passage to the Limit

Let $F\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$. By Lemma 1 there are finite linear combinations
$F_k\to F$ in $L^2$, and by Step 2

$$
F_k = \mathbb{E}[F_k] + \int_0^T g^{(k)}_s\,dW_s,
\qquad g^{(k)}\in\mathcal{L}^2.
$$

The stochastic integral has mean zero, so by the Itô isometry

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(F_k-F_l)^2\right]
= \left(\mathbb{E}[F_k-F_l]\right)^2
+ \mathbb{E}\int_0^T |g^{(k)}_s-g^{(l)}_s|^2\,ds.
$$

The left side tends to $0$ as $k,l\to\infty$, so $(g^{(k)})$ is Cauchy in
$\mathcal{L}^2$, which is complete, and converges to some $g\in\mathcal{L}^2$.
Also $\mathbb{E}[F_k]\to\mathbb{E}[F]$. Passing to the limit in $L^2$, using
the isometry again,

$$
F = \lim_{k\to\infty}F_k
= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T g_s\,dW_s.
$$

**Uniqueness.** If $\int_0^T g_s\,dW_s=\int_0^T \tilde g_s\,dW_s$, then by the
isometry $\mathbb{E}\int_0^T|g_s-\tilde g_s|^2ds=0$, so $g=\tilde g$
$dt\otimes d\mathbb{P}$-almost everywhere. This proves the Itô representation
theorem.

### Step 4: Martingales

Let $M$ be a square-integrable $\mathbb{F}$-martingale. Apply the Itô
representation theorem to $F=M_T\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$ to get
$M_T=\mathbb{E}[M_T]+\int_0^T g_s\,dW_s$. Since $M$ is a martingale,
$\mathbb{E}[M_T]=M_0$ and, taking conditional expectations and using that the
stochastic integral is a martingale,

$$
M_t = \mathbb{E}[M_T\mid\mathcal{F}_t]
= M_0 + \int_0^t g_s\,dW_s,
\qquad t\in[0,T].
$$

Uniqueness follows from the isometry as above. The right side is a continuous
process, which shows that $M$ has a continuous version. $\blacksquare$

## Application: Hedging

Consider the [[black-scholes-merton-model]] and a claim with payoff
$h(S_T)\in L^2(\mathbb{Q})$. Under the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb{Q}$ of
[[risk-neutral-pricing]] the process

$$
M_t = e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[h(S_T)\mid\mathcal{F}_t]
$$

is a square-integrable $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale in the filtration of the
$\mathbb{Q}$-Brownian motion $W^{\mathbb{Q}}$ (which equals the filtration of
$S$, since $S$ and $W^{\mathbb{Q}}$ determine each other). By the theorem,

$$
M_t = M_0 + \int_0^t g_s\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}_s
$$

for some $g$. The discounted stock price satisfies
$d(e^{-rt}S_t)=\sigma e^{-rt}S_t\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}_t$, so the strategy that
holds $\Delta_t = g_t/(\sigma e^{-rt}S_t)$ shares has discounted gains exactly
$M_t-M_0$. Starting from capital $M_0$, which is the price of the claim, this
self-financing strategy replicates the payoff. This shows that every claim can
be hedged, so the model is **complete**, and identifies the hedge ratio.

## Remarks

- The theorem depends on the filtration. It holds for the Brownian filtration,
  but not for a larger one: if $\mathcal{F}_t$ carries information that is
  independent of $W$ (for example a second independent source of randomness or
  a Poisson process), martingales need not be stochastic integrals against $W$.
- The integrand $g$ can be identified explicitly by the Clark-Ocone formula,
  $g_t=\mathbb{E}[D_tF\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$, where $D_tF$ is the Malliavin
  derivative, when $F$ is sufficiently smooth.
- The converse direction is immediate: every Itô integral of an $\mathcal{L}^2$
  integrand is a square-integrable martingale.
